stories.title: Astronauts install and unroll a new ISS solar array on the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the station
paragraphs: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed and deployed the second-to-last upgraded solar array for the International Space Station on Thursday, Oct. 29, Space.com reports. The Expedition 75 crewmates finished the 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk at 3:08 p.m. EDT (12:08 p.m. PT), working from the U.S. Quest airlock. According to Space.com, it was the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the station without a space shuttle docked, and the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019.

The rolled-up array, called an ISS roll-out solar array (iROSA), arrived earlier this month in the unpressurized trunk of SpaceX's Dragon cargo capsule on the company's 35th resupply mission for NASA. Space.com says Menon rode the end of the Canadarm2 robotic arm while carrying the 750-pound (340-kilogram) assembly to the station's port side, where the two astronauts bolted it onto the 2A power channel and connected its cables during a night pass for safety.

No motor was needed to unroll the array: the energy stored in its rolled-up carbon composite booms extended it to its full 63-foot (19-meter) length, Space.com reports. Mission Control called out the deployment about 4 hours and 23 minutes into the spacewalk, and the array was fully extended about 12 minutes later, partly covering the older panel on the P4 truss.

According to Space.com, the station's eight original arrays are producing less power after passing their 15-year design life, and the iROSAs used alongside them have raised the station's power supply by 20% to 30%. The extra power supports ongoing work and the station's planned controlled deorbit, currently scheduled for 2030. Working ahead of schedule, the pair also began preparing the final iROSA on its temporary platform.

stories.title: Artemis I data show radiation near the Moon is higher than in Earth orbit, but by less than expected
paragraphs: Tiny crystal detectors that flew around the Moon on NASA's uncrewed Artemis I mission in late 2022 have produced new measurements of the radiation astronauts would face there, ScienceDaily and Universe Today report. Orion carried more than 10,000 small crystals inside two human-shaped mannequins, including several dozen experimental fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors made at the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN) in Cracow, as part of the MARE experiment.

When charged particles pass through these crystals they leave defects that glow red under blue light, so individual particle tracks can be read under a fluorescence microscope without the chemical etching that plastic detectors need. After corrections and new background-removal software, the team's results differed by no more than 15% from conventional track detectors, and they also recorded many tracks below the threshold of older detectors.

Near the Moon, the doses were spread almost evenly through the mannequins, unlike an earlier space station experiment where low-energy protons trapped in Earth's Van Allen belts made doses uneven. 'Although total radiation doses near the Moon are higher than those in Earth orbit due to the considerable levels of galactic radiation, the difference is not as large as one might intuitively expect,' said co-author Pawel Bilski of IFJ PAN.

stories.title: Comets probably didn't deliver life's chemical building blocks to Earth, simulations suggest
paragraphs: A study published Oct. 28 in Scientific Reports argues that comets were an unlikely source of the chemicals that led to life on Earth, Science News and Universe Today report. Comets do carry carbon- and nitrogen-bearing molecules, and the idea that impacts seeded the young Earth with them has been around for a long time.

Richard Anslow and colleagues simulated whether hydrogen cyanide, a key starting molecule for prebiotic chemistry and one of the more robust ones, would survive a comet's trip through the atmosphere and its impact. On average, only one impact in more than a billion years would have delivered a meaningful amount. A comet would need to be larger than 100 meters, slow and arriving at a shallow angle, and it would have to hit land, since the ocean would dilute the molecules too quickly.

The authors also found that Earth's comet bombardment fell off quickly and that the atmosphere preferentially destroys small and oblique comets. Delivery may have been somewhat more likely on Mars, with its thinner atmosphere. Planetary geologist Gordon Osinski, who was not involved, told Science News that carbon-rich asteroids, volcanoes and hydrothermal vents are other possible sources and that he hopes others try to reproduce the results.
